In Figure 2.10, some terms are explained as follows:
• Keys: Refers to the Key vectors of the input sequence; each Key vector represents the
semantic information of a word
• Queries: Refers to the Query vectors of the input sequence; each Query vector represents
the semantic information of the word for which the attention weight is currently being
calculated
• Similarity: Refers to the similarity between the Key vector and the Query vector
• Linear Transformation: Refers to applying a linear transformation to the Key and Query
vectors
After the query and key transformations have been introduced, the next step is to see how they
are used inside self-attention. The self-attention mechanism combines queries, keys, and values
to calculate attention weights and produce a context-aware representation of each token.
Explaining the self-attention calculation
During the training process of the self-attention mechanism, the Scaled Dot-Product Attention
mechanism is a very core component. In this mechanism, the model first computes the similarity
between the Q vector and the K vector, then converts the similarity into attention weights via
the Softmax function, and finally multiplies the attention weights by the V vector to obtain the
final output.
Because the attention output depends on the Q, K, and V transformations, these matrices must
be learned during model training. The following subsection explains how the Q and K matrices
are initialized, updated through forward and backward propagation, and optimized to capture
context-specific relationships between tokens.
Training the Q and K weight matrices

The computation of scaled dot-product attention is shown in Figure 2.11.
Figure 2.11: Calculation of scaled dot-product attention
As seen in Figure 2.11, the process includes four steps:
1. Word embedding vectors. First, the input words are converted into word embedding
vectors, and then position encoding is added.
2. Q, K, V weight matrices. The word embedding vectors are multiplied by the weight matrices
Q, K, and V, respectively, to obtain the Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V).
3. Calculation of attention weights. The similarity between the Query (Q) and the Key (K) is
calculated, and then the attention weights are obtained by applying the Softmax function.
4. Weighted sum. The attention weights are multiplied by the Value (V), then summed to
get the attention output.

Chapter 2 45
In the transformer model, the transformation matrices are acquired by training the weight
matrices of Q and K. Specifically, the training process is as follows:
1. Initialization. Randomly initialize the weight matrices for Q and K.
2. Forward propagation
• Map the words in the input sequence to word embedding vectors
• Perform linear transformations on the K and Q vectors to obtain new K and Q
vectors
• Compute the similarity between the K and Q vectors
• Apply Softmax normalization to the similarity scores to obtain the attention
weights
• Perform a weighted sum of the V vectors based on the attention weights to obtain
the final output
3. Backpropagation
• Calculate the loss function
• Update the weight matrices of Q and K based on the loss function
4. Repeat steps 2 and 3 until training is complete
The goal of this training is to enable the transformer model to learn the similarity relationships
between words in different contexts. For example, in the sentence “Apple phone”, the Transformer
model should be able to learn that there is a higher similarity between “Apple” and “phone.” In
the computation process of the attention mechanism, both the Q vector and the K vector need
to undergo a linear transformation. The weight matrix of the linear transformation is shared,
meaning all words share the same weight matrix. The number of rows in the shared weight matrix
is equal to the size of the vocabulary; for however many words are in the vocabulary, that’s how
many rows are in the shared weight matrix. The number of columns in the shared weight matrix
equals the dimension of the word embedding vectors. The dimension of the word embedding
vectors determines the model’s capacity to express the semantic information of words. In practical
applications, the size of the shared weight matrix may be limited by computational resources.
Some techniques can be used to reduce the size of the shared weight matrix, such as parameter
pruning and knowledge distillation.
Understanding the Transformer Architecture Behind Large Language Models 46
Once the training process for the attention weight matrices is clear, the next step is to examine
the actual calculation performed during attention. Scaled dot-product attention explains how
similarity scores are computed, normalized, masked when needed, and then used to produce
the final weighted output.
Understanding scaled dot-product attention
The core principle of the scaled dot-product attention mechanism can be explained in the
following scenarios:
1. Compare the similarity of each word in a sentence with other words. This process is
achieved by computing the dot product between the Q vector of each word and the K
vectors of other words. The result of the dot product represents the similarity between
the two vectors; the higher the value, the greater the similarity. This process can be seen

as building a similarity matrix between words within a sentence.
The effect of similarity computation is shown in Figure 2.12.

vector space undergoes different spatial transformations during the training process
through deep learning.
2. After scaling, masking, and Softmax processing, attention weights are obtained. After
calculating similarity, the model performs scaling processing on the similarity to prevent
values from being too large or too small. Next, the model applies masking to the attention
weights to ensure that the model does not “see” words that have not yet been predicted.
Finally, the model applies Softmax to the scaled similarities to obtain the attention
weights. This process can be viewed as building a matrix of attention weights between
words within the sentence, identifying the key directions of similarity within the sentence
to better capture its semantic information. The effect is shown in Figure 2.13.
Figure 2.13: Example of similarity calculation based on scaled dot-product attention
(2)
Understanding the Transformer Architecture Behind Large Language Models 48
3. Calculate the weighted sum to obtain the final output. After calculating the attention
weights, the model multiplies the attention weights by the value (V) vectors and sums
them to get the final output. This process weights the word embedding vectors, making
their grouping with other phrases more distinct, as shown in Figure 2.14.
Figure 2.14: Example of similarity calculation based on scaled dot-product attention (3)
The result of the vector space transformation in the third step is significantly different from
those in the previous two steps. During the similarity calculation phase, we expect the word
embedding vector space to separate words with different meanings as much as possible, while
in the weighted sum phase, we want similar words to be clustered together to better predict the
probability of the next word. Why is it designed this way? Do you still remember the original intent
of the Transformer model? Its goal is to predict the probability of the next word, which aligns with
the goal of the large language models we use today. The model continuously tries to predict the
next word and adjusts its parameters based on the prediction to better anticipate the next word.

chunks.content:
Chapter 2 49
The output of the self-attention mechanism (i.e., the weighted values) is typically used as
intermediate representations in sequence processing tasks, and these representations are further
processed by subsequent network layers to predict the next word or perform other tasks. Thus,
the self-attention mechanism provides a flexible internal representation, offering each element in
the sequence a contextual representation that synthesizes information from the entire sequence.
The design of the Transformer model nests multiple identical processing layers. Through multi-
level data processing, the self-attention mechanism can capture representations at different
levels, for example, from individual words or characters to more complex semantic concepts
and relationships. Each layer is able to learn more abstract representations of information
from the previous layer’s output. This hierarchical processing helps the model understand the
complex structure of language, including syntactic and semantic information. With multilevel
data processing, the model not only distills information but also integrates and re-encodes
it to generate richer and more complex representations. This process involves capturing and
integrating information from different parts of the sequence to support complex reasoning and
comprehension tasks.
The discussion so far has explained how Transformer self-attention uses learned transformations,
similarity scores, normalization, masking, and weighted sums to build contextual token
representations. The next section extends this idea by showing how the Transformer uses multiple
attention heads in parallel, allowing the model to capture different types of relationships within
the same sequence.
Exploring the design of multi-head attention
In the Transformer model, the multi-head attention mechanism is implemented by combining
multiple attention mechanisms. Each attention mechanism is called a head, and multiple heads
work in parallel, with each head learning different representations. This mechanism enables the
model to focus on different parts of the sequence simultaneously when processing sequences. For
example, some heads may focus on the syntactic structure of the sentence, others may focus on
the semantic information, while others might focus on sentiment information. Through the
multi-head attention mechanism, the model can model sequences from different perspectives,
thereby enhancing its expressive and generalization capabilities.
Understanding the Transformer Architecture Behind Large Language Models 50
In the final layer of the model, the outputs of multiple heads are concatenated and then passed
through a linear transformation to obtain the final output. During this process, the model learns
the weights among the different heads in a deep learning manner, as well as how to combine the

chunks.content:
outputs from multiple heads. Building upon what was learned earlier, the following will introduce
the design details of the multi-head attention mechanism.
Figure 2.15: Structure of the multi-head attention mechanism
As shown in Figure 2.15, the multi-head attention mechanism actually consists of the following
three parts:
• Structure of the multi-head attention mechanism � The model is designed with a fixed
number of heads, and each head performs a linear transformation on the input Q, K, and
V. The linear transformations for each head may differ; these are actually implemented
by training weights. Linear transformations allow the model to capture key information
in different embedding spaces. For example, some transformations capture long-range
structural information while others capture short-range dependencies. This design enables
the Transformer model to consider multiple types of dependencies simultaneously when
processing sequential data.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 2 51
chunks.content:
Chapter 2 51
• Concatenating the attention outputs calculated by each head � The output of each head
is an independent attention vector, which are concatenated to form a long vector. The
reason for concatenating the attention outputs from each head is to merge the different
information captured by each head into a comprehensive representation. Since each head
may focus on different aspects of the input sequence, the concatenation operation allows
the model to utilize this diverse information in subsequent processing. The concatenated
vector contains information from all different heads, which is further integrated by a linear
layer to provide a unified output for downstream tasks. In the original Transformer model,
the number of heads is set to 8, and each head has a dimensionality of 64.
• Integrate information from multi-head attention through linear transformations,
ultimately outputting the attention representation. In the multi-head attention
mechanism, each head can independently learn features regarding the relationships
within the input. The linear layer is responsible for integrating these features, allowing
downstream network layers to utilize information from all heads for decision-making. The
linear layer not only performs weight scaling, but also incorporates non-linear activation
functions (such as ReLU) to enhance the model’s representational power.
Multi-head attention allows the Transformer to examine a sequence from several representational
perspectives at the same time. However, attention is only one part of the full architecture. The next
section brings the components together by showing how embeddings, positional information,
attention layers, feed-forward networks, residual connections, layer normalization, the encoder,
and the decoder form the complete Transformer model.
Assembling the transformer architecture
After examining word embeddings, positional encoding, self-attention, scaled dot-product
attention, and multi-head attention separately, we can now bring these components together
to understand the full Transformer architecture. At a high level, the original Transformer
was designed as an encoder-decoder model for sequence-to-sequence tasks such as machine
translation.
Understanding the Transformer Architecture Behind Large Language Models 52
The initial goal of the Transformer model was to build a “language translation” system. The
translation process can be represented as: Input Encoder module Decoder module
Output. The abstract structure of the Transformer is shown in Figure 2.16.
Figure 2.16: Abstract structure of the Transformer
The encoder and decoder are neural network modules that work together to transform an
input sequence into an output sequence. Each module contains multiple encoder and decoder
components. These components are connected in series and can be regarded as a multi-layer

chunks.heading: Chapter 2 51
chunks.content:
homogeneous network. In the earliest papers, this structure consisted of a 6-layer encoder-decoder
architecture. The structures of the Transformer encoder and decoder are shown in Figure 2.17.
Figure 2.17: Transformer encoder and decoder structure
Different Transformer-based models use different parts of this architecture: encoder-only models
such as BERT use the encoder stack, decoder-only models such as GPT use the decoder stack, and
encoder-decoder models use both.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 2 53
chunks.content:
Chapter 2 53
Each encoder contains multiple submodules, among which the core components are the self-
attention mechanism and the feed-forward neural network. The self-attention mechanism is
used to capture long-range dependencies within the sequence, while the feed-forward neural
network performs non-linear transformations on the information in the sequence. The internal
structure of the Transformer encoder is illustrated in Figure 2.18.
Figure 2.18: Internal structure of the Transformer encoder
The self-attention mechanism enables the model to consider all elements of the entire sequence
when processing each element within the sequence. This allows the model to capture dependencies
between any two elements in the sequence, regardless of their distance from each other. After
the self-attention mechanism captures the dependencies within the sequence, a feedforward
neural network (usually composed of two fully connected layers) independently applies nonlinear
transformations to the representation at each position. The feedforward neural network uses
the same parameters at all positions in the encoder layer, but these parameters are applied
independently to each position. This means that even if the inputs at different positions are the
same, the outputs after passing through the feedforward neural network may still be different.
Additionally, the self-attention layer and the feedforward neural network layer are integrated
through residual connections, which are typically followed by layer normalization to stabilize
training and accelerate convergence.
Summary
In this chapter, you learned why the Transformer model became the foundation of modern large
language models and how it improved on earlier approaches such as RNNs and LSTMs. You saw
that Transformers address major limitations of older sequence models—especially inefficient
sequential processing and difficulty handling long-range dependencies—by using self-attention
and parallel computation.
Understanding the Transformer Architecture Behind Large Language Models 54
You were introduced to the core structure of the Transformer, including its encoder-decoder
architecture, and to the major components that make it effective: word embeddings, positional
encoding, self-attention, multi-head attention, feed-forward networks, residual connections,
and layer normalization. You also learned why text must first be converted into numerical form,
how word embeddings capture semantic meaning, and how positional encoding helps preserve
word order.
A major part of the chapter focused on the attention mechanism. You learned how attention helps
the model determine which parts of a sequence are most relevant in context, how Q, K, and V
vectors are used to compute attention, and how scaled dot-product attention and multi-head

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 2 53
chunks.content:
attention enable the model to capture different kinds of relationships within language.
By the end of the chapter, you gained both a conceptual and structural understanding of the
Transformer—not only as a model originally designed for translation, but as the architecture that
powers today’s most important language models. This chapter prepared you to better understand
how modern AI systems process language through contextual understanding, efficient training,
and layered representation learning.
Building on this understanding of the Transformer architecture and its key mechanisms, you
are now ready to explore how this model evolved into modern generative systems. In the next
chapter, you will trace the path from the Transformer to GPT and ChatGPT, beginning with simple
language models such as the bigram model and gradually examining how autoregressive training
and large-scale pretraining enabled today’s conversational AI systems.
3
Tracing the Path from Bigram
Models to GPT and ChatGPT
In the evolution of natural language processing, the birth of the Transformer model marked
a significant turning point for deep learning technology. However, the original Transformer
model was not sufficient to support the generative demands of complex LLMs like ChatGPT. The
emergence of ChatGPT is the result of a gradual evolution based on the Transformer model. By
introducing innovations such as autoregressive pre-training, OpenAI expanded the Transformer
model—originally designed for machine translation—to a broader range of language generation
tasks. In this process, the GPT model, with its unique paradigm of pre-training followed by
fine-tuning and a design specifically aimed at text generation, opened a new chapter for LLMs.
This chapter will guide readers from the basics of bigram models, gradually exploring the core
principles of GPT, and revealing how it evolved step by step into ChatGPT.
We will be covering the following main topics in this chapter:
• Tracing the evolution from transformer to ChatGPT
• Building a basic bigram language model
• Understanding how GPT models generate text
• Improving GPT model training and generation
Tracing the Path from Bigram Models to GPT and ChatGPT 56
Tracing the evolution from transformer to ChatGPT
The original Transformer model was not designed for the kind of multi-turn conversation that
ChatGPT supports today. So how did one evolve into the other? This chapter will start from the
basic principles of the Transformer model, gradually introduce the fundamental concepts of
ChatGPT, and finally explain how to use the ChatGPT model for dialog generation tasks.
The Transformer model was first proposed by Google to solve the problem of machine translation.
This model is based on large-scale parallel corpora (such as English-French sentence pairs)

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 2 53
chunks.content:
and learns by minimizing the cross-entropy loss between the model’s predicted next-token
probabilities and the true next tokens. Based on this, OpenAI proposed the GPT model, extending
the Transformer architecture to a broader range of natural language processing tasks. GPT stands
for Generative Pre-trained Transformer. Like the Transformer, GPT is based on the Transformer
architecture, but its core idea is to use unsupervised pre-training on large-scale corpora to learn
deep language representations, followed by fine-tuning with a small amount of adaptive training
to complete specific downstream tasks. GPT differs structurally from Transformer in that GPT
only uses the decoder part of the Transformer, mainly for generative tasks such as text generation
and dialog generation.
The initial version of the Transformer model was trained on one-to-one parallel corpora,
had limited data, and could only be applied to machine translation tasks. To break through
this limitation, OpenAI proposed a new pre-training method, which trains the model in an
autoregressive manner and combines both masked prediction and next sentence prediction
strategies to enable the model to learn the structure of language directly from large amounts of
unlabeled text. The core idea of autoregressive pre-training is to give a sequence and generate
its elements step by step. This method makes use of large-scale text data and can be applied to
a variety of natural language processing tasks.
Masked prediction means randomly masking some words in the text sequence and requiring
the model to predict the masked words to learn the contextual relationships between words.
Next sentence prediction means that given a text sequence, the model judges whether the
next sentence is related to the given text, helping the model learn logical relationships between
sentences. GPT was the first model to adopt the autoregressive pre-training method and achieved
excellent results. Subsequently, improved models such as BERT and RoBERTa also adopted similar
pre-training methods.

Chapter 3 57
This chapter focuses on the GPT and ChatGPT models and analyzes them from the following
aspects.
Fine-tuning pre-trained models is a common approach in current LLM applications. The GPT
model adopts a pre-training plus fine-tuning paradigm, which was subsequently widely applied
to various natural language processing (NLP) tasks. Pre-trained models learn general language
characteristics from large-scale corpora and are then fine-tuned on specific tasks, significantly
improving the model’s performance and efficiency.
LLMs have a wide range of applications. GPT and its subsequent versions have demonstrated
outstanding performance on various natural language processing tasks, including text generation,
translation, summarization, question answering, and more. This shows that a single pre-trained
model, through fine-tuning, can be adapted to multiple tasks, significantly enhancing the model’s
versatility and flexibility.
The consensus is that the larger the number of parameters, the more powerful the capability. The
latest GPT model, with its enormous scale, has showcased the potential of LLMs in understanding
and generating natural language, driving the development of large-scale language model research
and sparking widespread discussions about the possible impacts of LLMs.
Next, a bigram model will be introduced as the starting point for language model training. Then,
the basic principles of the GPT model will be described, including the structure of GPT, pre-
training methods, and so on.
Building a basic bigram language model
The Bigram Model is one of the simplest language models. Based on the Markov assumption, it
assumes that the occurrence of a word is only related to the previous word. The core of the Bigram
Model is that, given a text sequence, the model needs to predict the next word.
When training the model, how can text be converted into numbers that can be computed? A
common method is to construct a dictionary that maps characters or words to numerical indexes.
In this way, the text sequence can be transformed into a sequence of numbers and input into the
model for training. During model prediction, numeric indexes can be converted back to characters
or words to obtain the model’s output.
Tracing the Path from Bigram Models to GPT and ChatGPT 58
This method is widely used in natural language processing and is fundamental to building text
datasets. This example uses character-level tokenization for simplicity. In this approach, each
character is treated as a token and mapped to a numerical index. This works reasonably well for
demonstrating the basic mechanics of language-model training, especially with Chinese text,
where individual characters can carry meaningful information. However, production GPT-style
models usually do not rely on simple character-level tokenization. Instead, they typically use

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 3 57
chunks.content:
subword tokenization methods such as Byte Pair Encoding (BPE), WordPiece, or SentencePiece,
which split text into reusable word pieces and handle large vocabularies more efficiently. For
real applications, libraries such as tiktoken or sentencepiece can be used to implement more
practical tokenization workflows.
The following sample demonstrates how to convert text into numerical indexes. Collect the file
“Three Hundred Tang Poems”, which contains multiple poems from the Tang Dynasty. The goal
is to train a model so that it can automatically generate Tang poetry.
The training data is as follows: each Tang poem is treated as a sentence, and these sentences are
concatenated to form a long text. The input to the model is this long text, and the objective is to
predict the next word. Issues to be solved in the process include how to convert text to numbers,
how to design the model, and how to train the model.
The first step in this workflow is data representation. Before the model can learn from text, the
text must be converted into numerical form so that it can be processed by the neural network.
The following subsection shows how the corpus is read, how the character vocabulary is created,
and how characters are mapped to numerical indices.
This chapter uses Three Hundred Tang Poems as a small character-level text corpus to
demonstrate the mechanics of language-model training. To make the example easier
for readers to follow, the Tang poetry referenced in the explanation and generated
examples has been translated into English. The same workflow can be applied to
other text corpora as well; for example, readers may use an English public-domain
corpus such as Shakespeare’s works or WikiText-2 by changing the dataset path,
tokenization choices, and generated text examples.

txt_file='tang_300_new.txt'

Next, establish a mapping table from characters to numbers to convert text into numbers. At the

numbers to characters is also required. The mapping table is shown below:
# Build the mapping from characters to numbers and from numbers to
characters
char_indices = dict((c, i) for i, c in enumerate(chars))
indices_char = dict((i, c) for i, c in enumerate(chars))
# Basic function for converting text into numbers
def text_to_indices(text):
return [char_indices[c] for c in text]
def indices_to_text(indices):
return ''.join(indices_char[i] for i in indices)
After the text has been converted into numerical indexes, the next step is to define a model that
can learn from those indexes. In a bigram language model, the design is intentionally simple:
the model receives the current token, converts it into an embedding, and predicts the next token.
This simple structure makes it easier to understand the basic prediction loop before moving on
to GPT-style models.
How to design the model
How can an LLM automatically generate a piece of poetry? Similar to ChatGPT, generating a
paragraph of text according to instructions is relatively complex, so the goal can be simplified to:
“Give a random word as input, and let the LLM automatically generate a new poem.” Recalling
the text generation effect of the LLM used, does it output word by word? The process of gradually
generating the same sentence is actually a continuous prediction process.

miles of clouds and moon.”

In this example, the model is implemented at the character level for simplicity: each

Understanding how GPT models generate text
The prediction process in a bigram model considers only the relationship between the current
token and the next token. In practical language generation, however, a model needs to use a wider
context to understand dependencies across a sequence. GPT models address this limitation by
using a decoder-only Transformer architecture with masked self-attention, positional embeddings,
and stacked Transformer blocks. This section explains how GPT extends the next-token prediction
loop introduced in the bigram model, then shows how the main components of a simple GPT-
style model can be implemented in code.

Structure of the GPT model
The GPT model extends the bigram model in three main ways. First, instead of looking at only
the previous one token, GPT uses self-attention to consider all previous tokens within the context
window. Second, GPT stacks multiple Transformer blocks instead of relying on a single embedding
layer and linear output layer. Third, GPT adds positional embeddings so the model can understand
where each token appears in the sequence. The core training loop remains similar to the bigram
example: the model predicts the next token, the prediction is compared with the target using
cross-entropy loss, and the parameters are updated through optimization.
Traditional Transformer models rely on large amounts of labeled data for training, which requires
substantial manual annotation and is costly. Researchers at OpenAI proposed a method that

and their positional relationships in the sequence.
• Masked Multi-Head Self-Attention: This is a key mechanism in the Transformer
model, used for handling language modeling tasks during the pre-training phase. This
mechanism allows the model to consider previous words when predicting the current

the training process. It normalizes the activations of each layer for each sample, helping
to prevent vanishing or exploding gradients.
• Feed-Forward Neural Network: This is another key component in the Transformer model,
used for feature extraction and mapping after the multi-head self-attention mechanism.

The basic definition of a single self-attention model includes 5 parts:
• Query: The main function of the query is to compute its compatibility or similarity with
each key. Each query corresponds to an element (or a time step) in the input sequence
and is used to compare with all keys to determine which parts of the sequence the model
should focus on.
• Key: The key is used to match with the query and generate a score (usually computed
via dot product), which reflects the degree of correlation between each query and the
elements in the sequence.
• Value: In the self-attention mechanism, each input element (such as a word or a point in
a time series) has a corresponding “value” vector, which carries important information
about that element. After the attention weights for each element (i.e., which elements
are more important and should be attended to) are calculated, these weights are used to
weight the “values.” The weighted “values” are then combined, forming the final output
that represents an integrated expression of the entire input sequence.
• A Buffer: The buffer is used to store a lower-triangular matrix, which is utilized to mask
future information when computing attention scores.
• A Dropout Layer: Dropout refers to randomly dropping some neurons during neural
network training, which helps to reduce the complexity of the network and thereby prevent
overfitting.
The matrices for queries, keys, and values are typically dense matrices with a size of n_embd ×
head_size. These three linear layers are updated constantly through the model’s training process,
enabling the model to better learn patterns and relationships within the input data. This learning
and adjustment are achieved through optimizing the loss function, performing backpropagation,
and updating the weights. In the absence of bias terms, each linear transformation relies only
on its weight matrix, thereby reducing the number of model parameters and, at times, helping
to avoid overfitting.

the original dimension of k is (B, T, hs), after the transpose it becomes (B, hs, T). The purpose
of this is to align the feature dimension of the key matrix with the time dimension of the query
matrix, so as to compute the dot product between each query vector and all key vectors.
Matrix multiplication
q@k.transpose(-2, -1): Here the @ symbol is used to perform batched matrix multiplication. The
query matrix q is multiplied by the transposed key matrix k, resulting in a new three-dimensional
matrix (B, T, T). Each element (b, i, j) in this matrix represents the dot product between the i -th
query vector and the j -th key vector in the b -th sample, namely the attention score of query i to
key j.

Masked self-attention is another part worth noting:
wei = wei.masked_fill(self.tril[:T, :T] = 0, float('-inf')) # (B, T, T)
This line of code uses a lower triangular matrix to mask future information. In the self-attention
mechanism, when the model predicts the current word, it can only refer to previous words and
cannot “see” future words. This masking mechanism is critical for text generation and the
understanding of language models. Here, a lower triangular matrix is used to mask future
information; that is, future information is set to negative infinity, so when computing the softmax,
the corresponding weights of future information become 0, thereby achieving the masking of
future information.
A detailed explanation of the above computational logic is as follows:
• Extracting the lower triangular matrix: self.tril[:T, :T]. This operation extracts
the first T rows and T columns of the lower triangular matrix to ensure it matches the
dimensions of the attention score matrix wei.

• Masking operation: self.tril[:T, :T] == 0. This step generates a boolean matrix
where the positions with 0 in the lower triangular matrix (i.e., above the diagonal) are
marked as True, and the rest as False.
• Filling operation: The wei.masked_fill function replaces the positions in the wei matrix,
where the boolean matrix is True, with a specified value, here float('-inf') (negative
infinity). This means that, before applying the softmax function, all positions with an
invalid causal relationship (i.e., a time step should not be able to “see” information from
subsequent time steps) are set to negative infinity.
This code successfully prevents information from leaking forward by setting the attention scores
for future time steps to negative infinity. When executing the softmax function, the exponentials
of these negative infinity positions are close to 0, thereby ensuring every time step can only attend
to itself and previous time steps.

The final step of the self-attention mechanism is to compute the weighted logic.
out = wei @ v # Matrix multiplication dimension transformation comment (B, T, T) @ (B, T, hs)
-> (B, T, hs)
Where, the variable explanations are as follows.
• wei: The attention score matrix obtained by calculating the dot product of the query (q)
and key (k), with dimensions (B, T, T), where B is the batch size and T is the sequence
length.
• v: The value matrix, with dimensions (B, T, hs), where each row represents the value
vector for the corresponding time step. These vectors contain information from the input
sequence and are weighted according to the computed attention weights.
A detailed explanation of the above operation is as follows:
Matrix multiplication is performed in batch using the @ symbol. In this operation, wei has
dimensions (B, T, T), and v has dimensions (B, T, hs). The resulting matrix out has dimensions
(B, T, hs).
For each batch (each B), the output at each time step T is calculated by performing a weighted
sum over all value vectors v across time steps, where the weights are provided by wei. Specifically,
each element (b, i, j) in the output is computed through a weighted sum between wei[*b*, *i*,
:] and v[*b*, :, *j*].
In this step, each row in wei serves as a set of weighting coefficients, which are used to compute
a weighted combination with all rows (value vectors) in v, yielding a weighted value vector that
reflects the model’s summary of the information that should be attended at each time step. This
process essentially applies the attention mechanism’s weights to the value vectors. The final
out output provides a representation that synthesizes information from the entire sequence, with
each time step’s information dynamically weighted based on prior (and current, if no mask is
used) information.

Adding special tokens to mark sequence boundaries
To achieve this, four types of special symbols are introduced: start symbol, end symbol, padding
symbol, and unknown symbol. During sample processing, each symbol (including comma, period,
question mark, etc.) is converted into a corresponding index number for easier model processing.
By learning these special symbols, the model can better understand input data and generate
fluent poetry. Since there are no specific characters to denote the start or end, user-defined special
symbols can be added at the beginning and end of the poem. In this way, the model will learn the
meaning of these symbols during training, and thus generate poetry that meets specifications.
Generally, the start symbol is set as "<start>", the end symbol as "<end>", the padding symbol
as "<pad>", and the unknown symbol as "<unk>". The introduction of start and end symbols
helps the model to better understand and process input data, enhancing training effectiveness;
the padding symbol helps handle inputs of different lengths; the unknown symbol increases
the model’s capability to handle unknown inputs, enhancing its generalization ability.

Applying early stopping to reduce overfitting

Using reinforcement learning to guide text generation
Reinforcement learning is a machine learning method that learns to take actions in an environment
by observing environmental feedback. During the process of model training, reinforcement
learning methods can be used to optimize the model’s generation logic in order to generate
poems that better conform to the required norms. This process typically involves monitoring the
quality of poems generated by the model and adjusting the model parameters to improve the
generation performance. For example, if there are non-compliant phenomena in the generated
poetry, such as consecutive punctuation marks or repeated words, reinforcement learning can
be used to adjust the model parameters and enhance the generated results. The reinforcement
learning implementation process for consecutive punctuation marks and special symbols includes

Techniques to LLMs
With the support of massive amounts of data and large-scale computing resources, we can build
a foundational LLM using GPT models. Foundational LLMs are capable of handling a variety of
tasks, such as text generation, text classification, text summarization, and text translation.
However, in practical applications, foundational LLMs often do not perform ideally on tasks in
vertical domains. For example, when applying a pre-trained LLM to a knowledge Q&A task in
the specific field of financial services, the model may underperform due to the lack of training on
business domain knowledge specific to a particular company. In order to adapt the pre-trained
LLM to a specific task, we need to take additional technical measures. One such approach is to
fine-tune the foundational model to optimize its performance for the target task. This chapter
will introduce fine-tuning techniques for pre-trained LLMs.
In this chapter, you will cover the following topics:

Applying Efficient Fine-Tuning Techniques to LLMs 98
Understanding fine-tuning for LLMs
Fine-tuning is a machine learning technique aimed at applying a model pre-trained on large-scale
datasets to specific tasks. Its purpose is to adapt the model to the data distribution of the target
task and thus improve its performance on that task. The fine-tuning process typically includes
the following five steps:
1. Clean and process the new dataset, usually splitting it into training, validation, and test
sets according to a certain ratio
2. Adjust the structure of the pre-trained model, typically by adding new layers on top or
modifying parts of the network structure
3. Set fine-tuning hyperparameters, such as learning rate, batch size, etc.
4. When training the model with the new dataset, use the validation set to adjust the model’s
hyperparameters
5. Use the test set to evaluate the performance of the model
Before introducing model fine-tuning, let us first review the inference process of LLMs. The
inference process of LLMs involves inputting a text sequence and having the model generate

which are obtained through pre-training on large-scale datasets and thus contain vast amounts
of knowledge. The inference process is shown in Figure 4.1.

In Figure 4.1, X represents the result of vectorizing the input text, which has three dimensions:

The model output Y is the text sequence generated based on the input text. During the inference
process, the model parameters W remain fixed and do not change. Therefore, the model output
Y is generated based on the input text X and the model parameters W.

Chapter 4 99
Once the basic fine-tuning process is clear, the next step is to compare the main ways a pre-trained
model can be adapted. Fine-tuning methods differ mainly in how much of the model they change:
some update all model parameters, some update only a small number of task-specific parameters,
and some intervene in the model’s internal representations instead of directly modifying its
weights.
Comparing fine-tuning approaches
Fine-tuning approaches can be understood as a spectrum of adaptation strategies. At one end,
full-parameter fine-tuning updates the entire model and can be effective but expensive. In the
middle, parameter-efficient methods update only selected modules or added parameters to reduce
training cost. At the other end, representation fine-tuning adapts model behavior by intervening in
hidden representations rather than retraining the full model. The following subsections compare
these approaches and explain when each type is useful.
Full-parameter fine-tuning
Full-parameter fine-tuning is the earliest form of fine-tuning technology. It adjusts all the
parameters of a pre-trained model with data from a specific task, enabling the model to adapt to a
new task. As current pre-trained LLMs have increasingly large parameter scales, the computational
cost of full-parameter fine-tuning has become prohibitively expensive and is no longer suitable
for conventional fine-tuning tasks.
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning
To address the excessive computational resources required for full-parameter fine-tuning,
parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) technology was developed. PEFT aims to achieve
efficient transfer learning by minimizing the number of parameters to be fine-tuned and reducing
computational complexity. It only updates a portion of the model’s parameters, significantly
lowering training time and cost, making it suitable for scenarios with limited computational
resources. PEFT techniques include Adapter Tuning, Prefix Tuning, Prompt Tuning, P-Tuning,
LoRA (Low Rank Adaptation Tuning), and various other methods that can be flexibly chosen
according to different tasks and model requirements. The following methods are common PEFT
strategies that reduce the number of trainable parameters in different ways.
Adapter fine-tuning
This method designs adapter structures and embeds them into the Transformer, fine-tuning
only the newly added adapter modules while keeping the original model parameters fixed. This
introduces a small number of additional parameters while maintaining efficiency.
Applying Efficient Fine-Tuning Techniques to LLMs 100
Prefix tuning
Prefix tuning is a PEFT technique that adds trainable virtual tokens as a prefix to the input,
updating only the prefix parameters while keeping the rest of the Transformer fixed. This method

chunks.heading: Chapter 4 99
chunks.content:
reduces the number of parameters to be updated and improves training efficiency.
Prompt tuning
Prompt Tuning is a simplified version of prefix tuning, achieved by adding prompt tokens at
the input layer. As the model size increases, the effect of Prompt Tuning can approach that of full
fine-tuning while avoiding complex machine learning processes.
P-tuning
P-tuning involves converting prompts into trainable embedding layers and processing them
with multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) and long short-term memory networks (LSTMs). This
approach addresses the impact of prompt construction on downstream task performance,
providing greater flexibility and stronger representational ability.
Low-rank adaptation (LoRA)
LoRA is a technique that introduces low-rank matrices into matrix multiplication modules to
simulate full fine-tuning. By updating key low-rank dimensions in the language model, it enables
efficient parameter adjustment and reduces computational complexity.
The methods discussed so far mainly adapt a model by updating either all parameters or a
smaller set of added or selected parameters. Representation fine-tuning takes a different route:
instead of focusing on weight updates, it attempts to influence the model through the internal
representations produced during processing.
Representation fine-tuning
Representation Fine-tuning (ReFT) focuses on intervening in the ‘ hidden representations ’
of a language model during inference, rather than directly modifying its weights. ‘ Hidden
representations ’ refers to intermediate results computed in the hidden layers of the network.
These representations exist in the form of feature vectors, capturing abstract features and
semantic information from the input data. Such intervention can be achieved in various ways,
such as linear transformations, nonlinear transformations (various activation functions), attention
mechanism adjustments, or context-aware adjustments.

Chapter 4 101
The core concept of ReFT originates from research on the interpretability of language models,
which shows that rich semantic information is encoded in the representations learned by these
models. By intervening in these representations, ReFT aims to unlock and leverage this encoded
knowledge to achieve more efficient and effective model adaptation.
After comparing the main categories of fine-tuning, the chapter now looks more closely at several
techniques that are widely used in practice. The next section explains how adapter fine-tuning,
prefix tuning, LoRA, and QLoRA work, showing how each method adapts a pre-trained model
while managing training cost, memory usage, and task-specific performance.
Exploring key fine-tuning techniques
After comparing the main categories of fine-tuning, it is useful to examine how several widely
used techniques work in practice. Adapter fine-tuning, prefix tuning, LoRA, and QLoRA all aim
to adapt a pre-trained model without updating every parameter, but they do so in different ways.
The following subsections explain how each technique modifies or extends the model, what
problem it is designed to solve, and why it matters for efficient LLM adaptation.
Adapter fine-tuning
Adapter fine-tuning, as a transfer learning method, was first proposed by Housby et al. in their
paper. The core idea is to add a small adapter layer on top of a pre-trained model to adapt to the
data of a specific task. The adapter layer is a small neural network, usually composed of linear
layers and activation functions. As the adapter layer contains few parameters, the training cost
is low. During the fine-tuning process, only the parameters of the adapter layer are updated,
while the parameters of the pre-trained model remain unchanged. In this way, the knowledge of
the pre-trained model is preserved while adapting to the data of specific tasks. The advantage of
adapter fine-tuning is that it can optimize the performance of the pre-trained model on specific
tasks without significantly increasing the number of parameters. Its disadvantage is that the
design of the adapter layer requires a certain degree of experience, and different tasks may need
different adapter layer designs.

According to the left side of Figure 4.2, two adapter layers are added in each Transformer. The

Adapter fine-tuning improves efficiency by adding small trainable modules inside the model.
Prefix tuning takes a different approach: instead of inserting adapter layers into the Transformer,
it adds trainable task-specific vectors before the input so that the model can be guided without
changing its original parameters.

Prefix tuning
The design inspiration for prefix tuning comes from the prompt-based guiding method in LLMs,
which adds instructions and examples before the task input to guide the model’s output generation.
However, different from prompt-based guiding, prefix tuning adds learnable prefixes before the
model input to guide the model in generating outputs. The advantage of this approach is that
it can learn prefixes to guide the model to produce more accurate outputs without the need to
design complex prompts. A schematic diagram of the prefix vector space is shown in Figure 4.3.
Figure 4.3: Schematic diagram of the prefix vector space
Tokens in prefix tuning refer to a series of continuous, task-specific vectors (i.e., prefixes) added
in front of the input sequence. These vectors are trainable parameters in the model that do not
come from the original language model parameters nor from any real vocabulary or text data.
Prefix vectors are randomly initialized and optimized during training using the backpropagation
algorithm. It can be seen that prefix tuning introduces small continuous parameter vectors to
provide the model with additional task-specific adaptability while keeping the pre-trained model
parameters unchanged.
Additionally, prefix tuning allows the model to support multiple tasks simultaneously, with each
task having an independent prefix. It can also process samples from multiple users or tasks within
a single batch, a feature not found in other lightweight tuning methods.
Prefix tuning shows how a model can be adapted by learning additional input-side vectors. LoRA
extends the same goal of efficient adaptation to the model’s weight matrices. Rather than training
the full set of model parameters, LoRA introduces low-rank updates that approximate the effect
of full fine-tuning with far fewer trainable parameters.
Applying Efficient Fine-Tuning Techniques to LLMs 104
LoRA
The core idea of LoRA fine-tuning is to keep the pre-trained model parameters unchanged and
improve the performance of LLMs on specific tasks by training a weighted matrix. The relationship
between pre-trained weights and fine-tuned weights is shown in Figure 4.4.
Figure 4.4: Relationship between pre-trained weights and fine-tuned weights in LoRA fine-
tuning
The parameter matrix on the left side of Figure 4.4 is the parameter matrix of the pre-trained model,
which remains unchanged during training; the matrix in the middle is the parameter matrix that
needs to be trained during fine-tuning. During fine-tuning, a weighted matrix is trained so that the
result of multiplying the pre-trained model’s parameter matrix by the parameter matrix trained
during fine-tuning better adapts to the data of specific tasks. In this way, the knowledge of the
pre-trained model is retained while being able to adapt to the data of specific tasks.

Research by Armen Aghajanyan et al. found that there is an inherent low-rank matrix structure
in pre-trained LLMs, which can simulate the effect of full fine-tuning with only a small number
of parameters. This technique effectively reduces the dimension of the matrix, thereby reducing
the number of parameters. Its low-rank decomposition is shown in Figure 4.5.
Figure 4.5: Illustration of low-rank decomposition
The advantage of LoRA is that it enables the optimization of the pre-trained model for specific
tasks without significantly increasing the number of parameters. The disadvantage of LoRA is
that it requires the design of an appropriate low-rank matrix, and different tasks may require
different designs.

chunks.content:
Chapter 4 105
LoRA reduces the number of trainable parameters, but fine-tuning very large models can still
require substantial GPU memory. QLoRA builds on LoRA by adding quantization, which lowers
the precision of model weights so that large models can be fine-tuned with much lower memory
requirements.
Quantization LoRA (QLoRA)
In the era of LLMs, even the smallest publicly available LLM parameters have reached 3 billion,
such as Microsoft’s Phi-3, which has 3.8 billion parameters, while the largest ones have already
exceeded 500 billion parameters (e.g., OpenAI’s GPT-4). Training and fine-tuning these
LLMs requires enormous computational resources and is often unaffordable. Therefore, PEFT
technology has become the mainstream fine-tuning technique. To further reduce GPU and memory
consumption, quantization technology is combined with LoRA, applying quantization to the LoRA
decomposition matrices, thereby further reducing parameter size. Research shows that a 16-bit
LAMA-65B model requires over 780GB of GPU memory during training, while QLoRA enables
fine-tuning on a single 48GB GPU machine while retaining 99.3% performance, and the training
time is greatly shortened to 24h.
How does QLoRA achieve this?
During the fine-tuning process, only the quantized parameters of the model are updated; all
other parameters remain unchanged. This approach not only preserves the knowledge of the
pre-trained model but also adapts to the data of specific tasks. The advantage of QLoRA is that
computation with quantized parameters is usually faster, especially on specialized hardware (such
as GPUs, TPUs), because low-precision computation can more efficiently leverage the hardware’s
parallel computing capabilities, improving computational efficiency and reducing the time cost
for training and inference.
After examining the principles behind adapter tuning, prefix tuning, LoRA, and QLoRA, the next
step is to see how these methods are supported in practical tooling. The Hugging Face PEFT toolkit
provides a common way to apply parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods to Transformer-based
models, making it easier to adapt large models while reducing training costs, memory usage, and
storage requirements.

This toolkit enables large pre-trained models to efficiently adapt to a variety of downstream

From Figure 4.8, it can be seen that the BERT model contains the encoder module, which consists
of 12 Transformer layers. In LoRA, it is necessary to specify which model layers to fine-tune, and
usually, all encoder layers are selected. After obtaining the above model structure, you can set
hyperparameters and the model layers to be fine-tuned in the LoRA config file. Relevant code is
shown as follows:
from lora_config import LoraConfig, TaskType
lora_config = LoraConfig(
task_type = TaskType.SEQ_CLS,
r = 8,
lora_alpha = 16,
lora_dropout = 0.1,
target_modules=["encoder.layer.*.attention.self.query", "encoder.
layer.*.attention.self.key"]
)
For better understanding, let’s explain the task type parameter (task_type). When using LoRA
for fine-tuning, the task type is used to specify the type of task for model fine-tuning. Common
task types include the following five:
• Sequence classification (SEQ_CLS): Used for sequence classification tasks, such as text
classification or sentiment analysis. Typical application scenarios include IMDB movie
review classification and sentiment analysis.
• Token classification (TOKEN_CLS): Used for token classification tasks, such as named
entity recognition (NER) or part-of-speech (POS) tagging. Typical application scenarios
include named entity recognition and tokenization.
• Sequence-to-sequence modeling (SEQ_2_SEQ_LM): Used for sequence-to-sequence
language model tasks, such as machine translation or text summarization. Typical
application scenarios include translation tasks and summary generation.
• Causal language modeling (CAUSAL_LM): Used for causal language model tasks, such
as generative tasks. Typical application scenarios include text generation and auto-
completion.
• Question answering (QUESTION_ANSWERING): Used for question answering tasks, such as
question answering systems on the SQuAD dataset. Typical application scenarios include
question answering systems and information retrieval.

The choice of the rank (r) for the low-rank matrix is related to the task, model size, dataset size,
and computational resources. According to comparative results, usually selecting r = 8 or r =
16 can cover most fine-tuning scenarios and achieve expected results.
lora_alpha is a scaling factor used to control the influence of the low-rank matrix on the original
weight matrix. It balances the adaptability and stability of the model by adjusting the output of
the low-rank matrix. Generally, the larger the value of lora_alpha, the greater the influence of
the low-rank matrix on the original weight matrix. In practical applications, this parameter is
usually set to 2 times the low-rank matrix parameter r.
lora_dropout is consistent with the random dropout function used during training, serving to
prevent overfitting. Typically, the value of lora_dropout is set to 0.1.
target_modules is a list used to specify which model layers need to be fine-tuned. In LoRA, only the
parameters of the model layers specified in target_modules will be updated, while the parameters
of other model layers remain unchanged. Usually, target_modules is set to the path of the model
layers that need to be fine-tuned. For example, encoder.layer.*.attention.self.query means
to fine-tune all self-attention query layers. According to actual test results, enabling LoRA on
all layers (including query weight matrices, projection layers, other linear layers in multi-head
attention modules, and output layers) performs better than fine-tuning only some layers.
After the main LoRA configuration parameters have been defined, the next step is to consider
how those settings affect training in practice. The following summary highlights the main
practical lessons for choosing data, selecting target layers, managing GPU memory, and avoiding
overtraining.
LoRA practical training summary
In actual training processes, we can summarize LoRA as follows:
• During fine-tuning, the quality requirements for the dataset are far higher than the
quantity requirements.
• Fine-tuning the entire model layer performs better than fine-tuning only specified layers,
but will result in greater GPU memory consumption. Conversely, if memory resources are
limited, you can fine-tune only some layers.
• Multiple rounds of iterative training may cause model degradation; it is recommended
to select an appropriate number of iterations based on actual conditions or use early

Applying fine-tuning to contract text classification
Previously, we provided a comprehensive introduction to the basic concepts of fine-tuning and
several key technologies related to it. In this section, we will demonstrate the application of fine-
tuning technology in a text classification task through a case study.
This case study demonstrates how fine-tuning can be applied to a practical contract text
classification task. It begins with a business scenario in which a law firm needs to classify
contract documents more efficiently, then walks through the full modeling workflow: preparing
the dataset, building a BERT-based classification model, defining the training and evaluation
pipeline, applying LoRA-based fine-tuning, and comparing model performance before and after
fine-tuning. The goal is to show how the fine-tuning concepts introduced earlier can be translated
into an end-to-end implementation.
John Doe is the head of a law firm, where the daily work involves a large amount of contract
text classification and retrieval. Usually, these tasks are performed manually by interns who
search, review, and match suitable contract texts for different business scenarios. Such work
is inefficient and prone to errors. To improve work efficiency, John Doe hopes to leverage deep
learning techniques to achieve automatic classification of contract texts. Driven by this need, we
first collected a large amount of contract text data and then built a text classifier using the BERT
model. We further optimized the BERT model through fine-tuning techniques to enhance its
performance in contract text classification tasks.
To implement this contract classification workflow, the first step is to build a baseline BERT-
based classifier that can process contract text, assign labels, and provide a model that can later
